title: Using a light-based scan to assess changes in the cervix during pregnancy and understand whether it could help predict when labour may start
official: Polarisation-sensitive Optical Coherence Tomography (PS-OCT) for assessing cervical remodelling changes predictive of spontaneous human birth
summary:
Background and study aims
The cervix is the lower part of the womb. During pregnancy, the cervix normally changes and softens as the body prepares for labour and birth. These changes are partly related to collagen, a strong protein that helps give the cervix its structure. At present, there is no simple clinic test that can directly assess how collagen in the cervix is changing during pregnancy.
This study will test a new light-based scanning device called polarisation-sensitive optical coherence tomography, or PS-OCT. The device is designed to assess collagen in the cervix. The aim of the study is to find out whether cervical PS-OCT can be used to obtain high-quality measurements, whether the measurements are repeatable, and whether women find the assessment acceptable during pregnancy. The study will also compare PS-OCT measurements with laboratory tests on cervical tissue samples.

Who can participate?
-Women aged 18 to 54 may be able to take part.
-The study includes non-pregnant women having a hysterectomy for a benign condition that is not related to cervical disease; pregnant women attending antenatal clinics or the preterm birth clinic who are between 20 and 28 weeks pregnant and may be at risk of preterm birth; and a smaller group of pregnant women from the study who will be invited to take part in an interview about their experience of the PS-OCT assessment.
-Women will not be able to take part in the pregnancy part of the study if they have a twin pregnancy, are unsure how many weeks pregnant they are, have a clinical vaginal infection, are currently taking antibiotics, have active vaginal bleeding, or have ruptured membranes.

What does the study involve?
The study has three related parts.
-In the first part, cervical tissue samples will be taken from women who are already having a hysterectomy for benign, non-cervical reasons. The tissue will be scanned using the PS-OCT device and then examined in the laboratory using microscope-based tests. This will help the researchers compare the PS-OCT findings with established methods for assessing collagen in tissue.
-In the second part, pregnant women will have a PS-OCT assessment of the cervix during a routine antenatal or preterm birth clinic visit between 20 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. The PS-OCT probe has a sterile disposable cover and is gently inserted into the vagina so that the cervix can be scanned. Four measurements will be taken from different areas of the cervix. For some participants, measurements may be repeated by the same or a second trained member of the research team to assess the consistency of the readings. Each set of readings is expected to take less than three minutes.
-In the third part, a smaller group of pregnant participants will be invited to take part in a questionnaire or semi-structured interview about their experience of the PS-OCT assessment. This will include questions about comfort, anxiety, embarrassment, any symptoms afterwards, and reasons for taking part. The interview will take place within 2 to 4 weeks after the PS-OCT assessment and may be by telephone or face to face.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
-Participants are not expected to benefit directly from taking part in this study. However, the information collected may help researchers develop better ways to assess changes in the cervix during pregnancy in future studies. This could help improve understanding of preterm birth risk and readiness for labour.
-The PS-OCT assessment uses light to scan the cervix and is considered low risk. The device uses a sterile disposable cover to reduce the risk of infection. Some women may find the vaginal assessment uncomfortable or embarrassing. There may also be minor discomfort similar to other vaginal examinations. Any adverse events or unexpected symptoms will be recorded by the research team.
-Participants can withdraw from the study at any time without giving a reason. Their decision will not affect their usual medical care or legal rights.

Where is the study run from?
The study is run from the Jessop Wing Maternity Unit at the Royal Hallamshire Hospital, Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, in collaboration with the University of Sheffield (UK).

When does the study start and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2026 to December 2027.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) Healthcare Technologies Investigator-led Research scheme and the Yorkshire MedTech Place-Based Impact Accelerator Application Fund (UK).

Who is the main contact?
Professor Dilly OC Anumba, d.o.c.anumba@sheffield.ac.uk

interventions.name: Cervical Polarisation Sensitive Optical Coherence Tomography (PS-OCT) Device (CervOScan)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Age >18 years, <55 years
Study A: Cervical tissue samples obtained from non-pregnant uterine specimens obtained at hysterectomy for benign non-cervical pathology (n = 10)
Study B: Feasibility/reproducibility studies of pregnant women at risk of preterm birth attending the antenatal clinics studied between 20 and 28 weeks gestation (n = 20)
Study C: Acceptability of cervical PS OCT during pregnancy (n=10, subset of Study B participants)
Exclusion criteria:
Study A: Surgery for cervical pathology or suspected genital tract cancer 

Study B:
1. Twin pregnancy
2. Inability to understand the study
3. Uncertain pregnancy duration
4. Established clinical vaginal infection
5. Current antibiotic treatment
6. Active vaginal bleeding
7. Ruptured fetal membranes
sponsor: Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
